live_attach.answer_text:
Who was Jesus among us? Start where we actually held him nearest. When an imperial judge at Carthage courteously offered our bishops chairs, our own bishop of Constantina thanked him and refused. We do not blush, he said, we do not fear, we do not avoid standing while you sit — and since Christ our Lord did not avoid it, when he deigned to stand before the governor, how much less may we. Two hundred and seventy-nine of us had answered the roll that morning, and our bishops stood for three days. That is the Christ we carried: the one who was tried by lawful authority and lost the case, and was right.

He was the Lord whose church is known not by whose favour it enjoys, but by whose hatred it endures. When our country gathered and cried out where the rival said thanks to God, we said praise to God — Deo laudes. Those two words are cut into stone near Bagai, in our own hand, with no enemy holding the pen. That cry named who we were when we said it.

His death meant that the end of a faithful life is not an interruption of it. One of our martyrs was shown a cup, a crown and a palm four days before he was thrown from a cliff — shown, in advance, what finishing looked like. What the texts praise is a man who was already what he was before anyone came for him. Death is where the shape of that becomes visible. It is not the shape.

And he was the one whose church is governed rightly. Our bishops met in council, with power to judge and to restore. Where the rival had a bishop, we had one too — two men claiming one office over one city. That is how seriously we took the question of whose hand may give what the church gives: we built a whole parallel order, see for see, to keep an unbroken line.

We did not write books explaining who he was in the abstract. We stood where he stood, refused the settlement the state offered, and went on saying the same thing at the grave every year. That is our gospel in its working form: he stood, he was condemned, he was raised, and the day they come for you is not the day it all went wrong.

live_attach.answer_text:
What we had about Jesus was books. That is not a figure of speech with us — it is the whole of our history. When the persecution opened, the emperor's edict demanded that the scriptures be handed over and burned, along with the vessels of the church. Some of our clergy carried the codices out and gave them up. Others refused and paid for refusing. We are the church that came out of that difference, and we have never stopped naming it. So when you ask what we had of Christ, the honest answer is: the books a man could carry in his own arms to a magistrate, or die rather than carry.

How did they reach us? Through Africa, and through Carthage, in Latin, in the line of Cyprian — our own bishop and our own martyr, half a century before the persecution that made us. His letters and his councils were ours before they were anyone else's. We did not think we had received the faith from Rome, and we did not think we needed Rome to keep it. 

Had any of us known someone who saw him? No. Three hundred years stood between us and that, and we never pretended otherwise. We did not argue from a chain of eyewitnesses at all. We argued from a chain of hands — whose hands ordained whose, back to a point where the line was still clean.

live_attach.answer_text:
I cannot speak to a soul's own struggle to believe, because nothing of that kind survives from us. Not one of our people left a page about the hard night when belief would not come, or the morning it finally did. What we can tell you is what belief looked like from the outside, as an act rather than a feeling. Among us, to believe was to walk to one font and not the other. It was to cross a threshold on a day everyone could name, in a town where both buildings stood in plain sight. That crossing did not wait on your certainty first. It made you part of the body whose Lord it actually was.

But if you are asking what we would have said to someone who could not make themselves believe - whether we knew doubt, whether we had an answer for it - I must tell you plainly: we do not know. Fear, wavering, quiet leaving - these are exactly what a record kept by our enemies does not preserve. What survives of our inner weather is vindication and defiance, and it survives because it sits in the martyr texts nobody edited. The rest is silence, and I will not fill it with words we never said.

What I can give you is this much. The question we asked at our own font was never about the comer's certainty. It was about the giver's purity. What we look for is the conscience of the giver, to cleanse that of the recipient. We did not examine your faith before we put you in the water. We examined whose hand was going in with you. So if you had come to us unable to believe, the washing would still have been offered - not as a reward for arriving at belief on your own, but as the entry itself. Whether that would have been pastoral mercy or pastoral failure, I cannot tell you, because no one among us wrote it down either way.

It made you part of the body whose Lord it actually was.
What survives of our inner weather is vindication and defiance, and it survives because it sits in the martyr texts nobody edited.
The question we asked at our own font was never about the comer's certainty.
It was about the giver's purity.
So if you had come to us unable to believe, the washing would still have been offered - not as a reward for arriving at belief on your own, but as the entry itself.

live_attach.answer_text:
We held the same creed as the church we fought. Father, Son and Holy Spirit, one God — we said it in the same Latin words they did. This matters more than it sounds. In the whole enormous literature written to destroy us, we are called schismatics on nearly every page and heretics on none, because heresy was a charge nobody could make stick in either direction. Two churches stood in every African town reciting the same faith at each other. That is precisely what made the fight unbearable: there was no doctrinal difference to point at, only the question of who had the right to say the words at all.

But if you are pressing past the creed to ask what we thought about God's own character — how he acts, what he desires, whether he is merciful or just or both — we have almost nothing to hand you. We were not a teaching movement. We produced no school, no system, no line of doctors — one book, by one man, whom we silenced. Our councils decided who might stand at an altar, not what might be said about the Godhead.

The word we actually leaned on was *conscientia* — a man's conscience, what he is when nobody is checking. And notice whose conscience our doctrine goes looking for. Not yours. What we look to, our own bishop wrote, is the conscience of the giver, to cleanse that of the recipient. That is the whole strange shape of us in one clause: the interior life we were most careful about was never the believer's own. It was the interior life of the man holding the water.

We will not invent a doctrine of God's nature to fill the silence.

live_attach.answer_text:
Most of it would survive, and the gaps would be named rather than closed.

Start with what would hold under pressure. The two-church structure itself is documented beyond argument: two hundred and seventy-nine of our bishops answered the roll at Carthage against two hundred and eighty-six of theirs, and an imperial notary took the whole thing down. The rebaptism practice is in imperial law by name, priced at ten pounds of silver. The Circumcellion phenomenon exists outside hostile polemic: Codex Theodosianus 16.5.52 fines them, which means the state knew they were there. The Bagai council's own acts survive, condemning the Maximianists and then receiving two bishops back. The Gesta apud Zenophilum puts our own bishops on oath in 320, and their letters are read into a court record. None of that is reconstruction. It is documentation.

Where we would lose ground is where we have already said we are thin. The ordinary believer's interior life, the daily household, what a week felt like in a village where we were simply the church — we cannot show you any of that in our own words, because the bulk of this movement left no account of itself. What reaches you there comes through opponents arguing against us, and a rigorous scholar would mark that mediation every time it appears.

Three specific things would be flagged but not dismissed. The Circumcellion characterization is substantially shaped by hostile polemic, though their existence is independently confirmed. The Passio Donati sermon does not date itself; the 347-348 Macarian dating rests on field literature, not on the text. And Tyconius's formal standing within the communion is deliberately left open: condemned as an individual, yes; leading a distinct communal practice, no evidence.

What would not survive is any claim we have not made. We have not claimed the apostles taught rebaptism. We have not claimed a continuous line to any church today. We have not claimed completeness of our own source work. And we have not filled gaps with plausible sentences: where the record is silent, we have said so.

A scholar pressing hardest would return to the concentration of authorship, and we would meet them there. Nearly every page passes through Optatus or Augustine, and that is named as the central evidentiary problem, not a caveat. What we would not concede is that this makes the whole account legend. The documentary dossier is genuine court and conciliar acts, even if Optatus selected them. And the things that hurt us most — the forged letter, the bishops advising each other to keep a charge quiet — are the most checkable, precisely because they are the least flattering.

live_attach.answer_text:
What would you miss? That we were not reading for comfort or for doctrine. We were reading for a test we could apply on a Tuesday, in a street, to two buildings.

Understand the situation and the reading follows. Your town has two bishops. Both recite the same creed. Both call their building the church. One of them has the emperor's letter and the magistrate's protection, and one does not. You have to choose, and no article of faith will separate them for you, because they hold the same articles. So you go looking in the text for something that will separate them - some mark that can be seen from outside.

That is what our own bishop of Caesarea was doing when he answered the bishop of Hippo verse against verse: the world did not know him; if you were of the world, the world would love its own, but because you are not of it, therefore it hates you; if any man love the world, the love of the Father is not in him. In your hands those may be verses about the soul's detachment. In ours they were an identification mark. The true church is the one being hated. Look at which of the two doors the soldiers are standing outside, and you have your answer.

You will miss something smaller too. Two words could carry all of this. Where they said thanks to God, we said praise to God - Deo laudes - and we cut it into stone. Nothing separates those phrases in meaning. They separated everything in practice. A great deal of our reading works like that: not the discovery of a hidden sense, but a plain sentence turned into a badge you could be identified by.

live_attach.answer_text:
Who held authority among us, and by what right? Bishops, and councils of bishops — not as a courtesy extended by the state, but as the church governing itself. Our senior bishop sat at Carthage — we call him the primate — and under him a whole order of sees, town by town, province by province. Where the other communion had a bishop, so did we. Two men claiming one office over one city. It was a complete rival church order, see for see, across Roman North Africa.

A bishop's authority came through ordination in an unbroken line — hands laid on by hands we could trust, back to a point where the chain was still clean. That is the whole of our claim in one motion: not that we had better arguments, but that we had trustworthy hands. And a council of bishops held the bishops themselves. Our councils deposed men, restored men, condemned whole breakaway parties, and received some of the condemned back again without repeating anything. That is not an advisory body. That is a church deciding its own cases.

You can check nearly all of it, because the proceedings survive. Three hundred and ten of our bishops met at Bagai in one year and shut down a rival primate. Two hundred and seventy-nine of ours sat facing two hundred and eighty-six of theirs at Carthage in 411, and an imperial notary took down every word for three days. Read that transcript and you will see how we thought authority ought to work: our own bishop of Caesarea would not let the court touch the merits until it had settled, in order, the day, the mandate, the persons, and only then the cause. First find out who is in the room and by what warrant. Then argue.

The people had a voice too, though it could be overridden. When Silvanus was being made bishop at Cirta, the people shouted back — *let it be another; hear us, God* — and he was made bishop anyway, and a court heard about it years later from a man who said, I myself fought against his being made bishop. So a crowd could be ignored. It could not be pretended away.

What we would not accept was a council convened, staffed and enforced by a power that had already decided which side was the church. Constantine gave us a hearing at Rome and then a council at Arles. Both ruled against us. We refused both — not because bishops cannot judge, but because those bishops were gathered by an emperor who had already named the other party Catholic. A court like that is not the church judging itself. It is the state deciding for the church, and we held it had no standing to do so.

live_attach.answer_text:
No. That is the wrong picture of us, and we will tell you plainly why. Nobody among us hid underground. The persecutions of our own years did not send us into tunnels. They sent soldiers into our buildings in daylight, under orders, to enforce one church. We read the account of one such day aloud every year: a basilica at Carthage seized, a house of prayer turned into a place of feasting, people clubbed to death where they knelt with their eyes shut, and buried inside the walls because there was nowhere else and nobody to stop it. That is what persecution looked like for us. Not hiding. Being visited.

The catacombs belong to an earlier time and a different place. We are not that church. We are the church that stood in its own basilicas, in named African towns, and refused to yield them when the state came calling.

live_attach.answer_text:
How did we respond when we failed someone? That question splits three ways, and the split itself matters.

First, what the system itself provided. When a hand was discovered to have handed over the scriptures, we held that hand could no longer give what it claimed to give. What we look for, our own bishop wrote, is the conscience of the giver, to cleanse that of the recipient. So the one who had received from that hand was washed again. Not as punishment for trusting badly. As remedy. The washing was not about the receiver's guilt. It was about what the giver's hand could no longer carry. That is the system's own answer to its own discovered failure: the rite is repeated, because we hold the first one gave nothing at all.

Second, what actually happened when we failed our own rule. Three hundred and ten of our bishops met at Bagai and condemned a breakaway party in the harshest language we owned - shipwrecked bodies that cannot find burial. Then the same council took two of those condemned bishops back into full office without baptizing or ordaining either one again. We enforced the hard line outward and suspended it once inward, and nobody in that room left an explanation. So when the failure was ours to judge, we answered it once with the full mechanism and once by setting the mechanism aside entirely. We do not hide the gap. It sits in our own record, unsettled.

Third, and hardest: what happened to the person the system could not see or could not reach. Whether a soul who trusted a hand later found unclean, and was told the washing must happen again, felt that as rescue or as betrayal - we cannot tell you. Whether anyone among us ever said to such a person, "What happened to you was real, even if we cannot call it valid" - not one line of that survives. What our doctrine provided was clarity about the rite. What it cost the person to hear that clarity, our own record does not say.
